bib.title: James–Stein Estimation and Ridge Regression (Computer Age Statistical Inference, chapter 7)

question: Why and how does deliberate bias (shrinkage) beat maximum likelihood when many parameters are estimated at once, and how does this carry over to ridge regression?

limits: No optimality theory for shrinkage: 'at present there is no optimality theory for shrinkage estimation' (p. 102); no foolproof way to choose the ridge parameter lambda.
JS gains depend on the coordinates being exchangeable: it hurts genuinely outstanding cases (Clemente) and the baseball gain is for total error, not each player.
The 18-player baseball data are partly artificial: the original 45 at bats per player were augmented with 45 binomial draws, which the authors say gives a less optimistic view of JS (p. 105).
JS guarantee in (7.44) assumes sigma^2 is known; if estimated, some of the improvement erodes (footnote 2, p. 102).
Ridge is not scale-equivariant, so predictors must be standardized first; the intercept is not penalized (note 4).
practices: Use James-Stein-type shrinkage rather than the MLE when estimating N >= 4 (or p >= 3 regression) parameters at once; B-hat = 1 - (N-3)/S shrinks toward the grand mean (p. 92-93).
Standardize predictors to mean 0 and sum of squares 1 before ridge, and do not penalize the intercept (eq. 7.35, note 4, p. 98, 106).
Take ridge lambda = 0 as OLS and lambda -> infinity as the zero vector; the larger lambda, the stronger the shrinkage (p. 98).
Prefer shrinkage for coefficient interpretation in correlated predictors, since ridge stabilizes standard errors (Table 7.3, p. 100-101).
Use limited-translation shrinkage (bound within one sigma0 of the MLE) to protect extreme cases while keeping most of the gain (eq. 7.47, p. 104).
Ask which 'others' to pool with: do not put an outstanding case in a shrinkage pool of ordinary ones (p. 103-104).

terms.definition: the plug-in version of the Bayes estimator (7.3): theta-hat_i = M-hat + B-hat (x_i - M-hat), with M-hat = x-bar and B-hat = 1 - (N-3)/S, S = sum (x_i - x-bar)^2
an estimator whose total squared error risk exceeds that of another estimator no matter what the parameter is
a Bayesian model leads to a Bayes estimator, which itself is estimated empirically (frequentistically) from all the data and then applied to individual cases
beta-hat(lambda) = (S + lambda I)^-1 X'y = (S + lambda I)^-1 S beta-hat; equivalently argmin of ||y - X beta||^2 + lambda ||beta||^2
generically, almost any method that tamps down statistical variability in high-dimensional estimation or prediction problems
penalized least squares with the l1 norm ||beta||_1 as penalty (eq. 7.42), Chapter 16
JS variant where shrinkage may not move an estimate more than one sigma0 unit from the MLE
learning from the experience of others: each batter learns from the other 17
